prompt: There's exactly one American, living or dead, who is NOT invited to the cookout. Name them and defend the exclusion.
response:
**Benedict Arnold.**

The defense practically writes itself: the cookout is fundamentally about loyalty — to the people, to the vibe, to the plate you promised to bring. Benedict Arnold is America's original "he switched up on us." You cannot have a man at the function who, at the first sign of a better offer, will hand the potato salad recipe over to the opposition. He didn't just leave the group chat; he sold the group chat's location to the British.

Everyone else, living or dead, gets at least a provisional invite under the cookout's core principle of redemption: you can show up, sit quietly by the coolers, prove yourself with a respectable dish, and maybe work your way up to grill-adjacent. Even history's most cookout-ineligible figures technically get the chance to be humbled in person — that's part of the punishment.

But Arnold uniquely fails the one unforgivable test: **he'd tell the other cookout where we are.** Everything else can be worked through. Espionage against the function cannot.

He can have a plate to go. Foil, no lid. That's the compromise.
